title: Oscillation and Reaction Board Techniques for Estimating Inertial Properties of a Below-knee Prosthesis
protocol: Determine each participant's preferred walking speed using a 20 m walkway.
Use a photocell-based timing system to measure time for approximately 5 meters in the middle of the walkway.
Repeat the measurement process five times to quantify preferred walking speed as the mean value.
Complete five successful overground walking trials while collecting ground reaction forces from two force plates and motion data from a six-camera system.
Ensure each trial is within ±3% of the participant's preferred speed without visible stride adjustments for force plate contact.
Place retroreflective markers bilaterally on the greater trochanter, lateral femoral condyle, lateral malleolus, lateral aspect of the heel, and head of the fifth metatarsal before data collection.
Use a three-segment sagittal plane inverse dynamics model to estimate resultant joint forces and moments at the hip, knee, and ankle.
Estimate segment inertial properties for intact body segments based on regression equations from de Leva8.
Measure inertial properties of the prosthesis and residual limb directly and distribute them between the prosthetic shank and foot.
Have the amputee sit in a chair where the prosthetic leg can be comfortably lifted off the seat.
Perform knee flexion and extension actions to identify the knee center of rotation (COR).
Place a small piece of tape at the identified knee COR.
Have the amputee stand to measure the distance from the top of the prosthesis to the knee COR.
Measure the distance between the knee COR and the ankle COR, assuming the ankle COR is similar to that of an intact ankle.
Remove the prosthesis and underlying sleeve.
Take measurements of the proximal circumference of the residual limb close to the knee joint.
Take measurements of the distal circumference of the residual limb at the last bony prominence on the distal end.
Measure the length of the residual limb from the fibular head to the most distal aspect.
Remove the axle to take out the inner cage from the oscillation rack.
Place the amputee's liner and ply within the socket of the prosthesis.
Securely position the prosthesis with shoe still on within the inner oscillation cage.
Use a Velcro strap to secure the foot of the prosthesis on the distal plate of the cage.
Reposition the inner cage within the oscillation rack.
Tighten the adjustable plates horizontally to secure the top of the prosthesis within the cage.
Secure the axle and align the suspending arm with the set screw for less than 5° angle setting.
Collect three oscillation trials by pulling the inner cage back until it hits the set screw, then move forward slightly.
Record the average time for one complete cycle of oscillation for each trial.
Measure the distance between the top adjustable plate and the fixed cross-member at the top of the inner cage using digital calipers or a flexible measuring tape.
Measure the distance between the bottom adjustable plate and the fixed cross-member at the top of the inner cage using digital calipers or a flexible measuring tape.
Measure the distance between the bottom adjustable plate and the fixed cross-member at the bottom of the inner cage using digital calipers or a flexible measuring tape.
Measure the length of the reaction board.
Position the rack and prosthetic limb in the reaction board setup.
Place one end of the inner cage over the scale.
Position the knife edge at the bottom of the inner cage to ensure it is level with no tension between the two knife edges.
Lift the scale-end several times and place it back down on the scale.
Record the consistent reading from the scale once achieved.
Remove the prosthesis from the inner cage.
Return the top and/or bottom plates to their original position if they were moved.
Repeat Step 1.8 to record the reaction board reading for just the cage.
Remove the shoe from the prosthetic limb.
Measure the mass of the shoe.
Measure the mass of the prosthesis without the shoe.
Take several measurements of the prosthesis.
Measure the distance between the center of rotation (COR) of ankle and the plantar surface of the foot.
Measure the length of the prosthetic foot without the shoe.
Place the shoe back on the prosthesis.
Measure the distance from the ankle COR to the sole of the shoe.
Measure the length of the foot with the shoe on.
Reposition the inner cage within the oscillation rack so that the black corner with reflective tape is closest to the photocell.
Secure the axis and align the suspending arm of the inner cage with the set screw to set the angle of oscillation to less than 5°.
Collect 10 oscillation trials.
Record only the first oscillation period of each trial.
Distribute the inertial properties of the prosthesis into a foot segment and a shank segment for inverse dynamics modeling.
Base the distribution on data from a dismantled prosthetic limb with a total mass of 2.126 kg, including a socket mass of 1.406 kg and a foot mass of 0.72 kg.
Apportion 66% of the prosthesis mass to the prosthetic socket and 34% to the foot.
Perform a sensitivity analysis to determine the effect on the estimated moment of inertia about the knee joint.
Compare the results with experimental measurements from Mattes et al. based on de Leva's distribution (foot = 24%, shank = 76%) which underestimates by approximately 5%.
Use percentages based on dismantled prosthesis data for foot (34%) and shank (66%) masses, resulting in an overestimation of the moment of inertia about the knee joint by approximately 2%.
Distribute prosthesis mass between prosthetic foot and socket segments based on measurements of a dismantled prosthetic limb.
Determine COM location of the prosthetic foot using regression equations for an intact foot.
Use results from sensitivity analyses by Miller to estimate resultant joint moments at the knee.
Estimate resultant joint moments at the knee using direct measurements of prosthesis inertial properties and regressions equations for an intact shank and foot.
Compare knee moment profiles obtained from different methods and subjects, noting differences less than 2% of peak knee moment during stance.
Dismantle multiple below-knee prostheses and balance the prosthetic foot on a knife edge to determine its COM location.
Compare results with estimates based on regression equations for an intact foot, noting little difference between the two.
Determine MOI of the prosthetic foot about a transverse axis through its COM using de Leva's regressions for an intact foot.
Express MOI of the foot relative to the knee joint using the parallel axis theorem.
